Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Shopowner
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Vignette:
Malia, a 66-year-old woman of Oceania heritage, divorced and living alone above the small convenience shop she had owned for thirty years, could still feel the exact weight of the evening air from two years ago. It had been just after dusk, the same soft hour when the streetlights flicker on and the shop traffic thins. She had stepped outside to bring in a display of woven baskets, a routine she had performed thousands of times, when two officers approached her. They said someone had reported a woman matching her description loitering near the back alley. Malia tried to explain she owned the store, that she was just closing up. She reached for her keys to show them, and in the next moment she was on the ground, her wrists twisted behind her back, a knee pressing into her spine. The world went grey and distant. She remembered the sound of her own voice saying “please,” but the next minutes were a blur she could never recover. She had tried, many times, to pull those moments back into focus, but there was only a dark patch where the details should have been, like a torn photograph. What she did remember—the grit of the pavement against her cheek, the officer’s heavy breathing, the way the streetlight above her seemed to pulse—felt too extreme to be real. Sometimes she caught herself thinking it must have happened to someone else, that her own mind had made it up. But the bruises on her ribs the next morning were real enough.

In the months that followed, Malia found herself unable to stay in the shop past four in the afternoon. As the light began to shift toward that particular dusk, her chest would tighten and she would feel a strange, floating dizziness, as if the floor were tilting beneath her. She began closing early, telling herself it was for inventory or that business was slow anyway. Her regular customers noticed, and some stopped coming altogether, assuming she was unwell or unreliable. She let them think what they wanted. What she could not explain was the way her own reflection in the shop window seemed to watch her, or how the feeling of being observed followed her even into her apartment, where she would sit in the dark with the blinds drawn, certain that someone was noting her every move. She had come to believe that her reaction to that night proved something fundamental about her: that she was inadequate, that a stronger person would have fought back or stayed calm, that a better coper would have moved on by now. The fact that she could not stop thinking about it, that she could not even describe what had happened without her voice catching and the words scattering, made her certain she was losing her mind.

She began to dread the anniversary of the event with a physical sickness that arrived weeks in advance. The date loomed like a storm she could not outrun, and each year she spent it alone in her apartment, refusing to answer the phone, unable to explain to her adult children why she could not see them. Her only comfort came in small, impulsive purchases—a new kitchen gadget she did not need, a pair of earrings she never wore, online orders for books she would not read. The packages arrived and she would feel a brief, hollow relief before the guilt set in. Her savings had begun to dwindle, and she had started hiding the credit card statements in a drawer.

What finally brought Malia to seek help was not the fear or the avoidance, but the isolation. She had realized, with a kind of quiet horror, that she had not had a real conversation with another person in nearly three weeks. A neighbor had knocked to ask if she was all right, and Malia had stood frozen behind her door, unable to answer, terrified that if she opened her mouth she would start screaming or crying or both. She made an appointment the next morning. She was not sure what she hoped for—only that she could not keep living this way, trapped in the hours between a memory she could not trust and a future she could not imagine.
